pos: n. (the northern archbishopric of England, whose cathedral school taught Alcuin and whose province kept its own rite until 1549)
etymology: From Latin Eboracum, a Brigantian name, through Old English Eoforwic and Old Norse Jórvík.
biblical_def: York is the second see of England and the metropolitan of its northern province, founded in 627 when Paulinus baptised King Edwin, and raised to an archbishopric in 735. Its cathedral school under Aelbert and then Alcuin was the best in Europe in the eighth century, and when Charlemagne wanted a master for his palace school he sent for Alcuin of York, who took the Northumbrian learning to the Continent and became the chief scholar of the Carolingian renewal. York kept its own liturgical use, distinct from Salisbury's, until the Prayer Book of 1549. Its archbishops included Thomas Wolsey, who never visited the diocese, and Edwin Sandys and Tobie Matthew, who preached incessantly. The dictionary records York for the school. A cathedral school in a damp northern town, with a library and a few good masters, supplied the man who re-founded education in the Frankish empire, which is the ordinary way the church's learning has always moved: by one teacher handing a method to the next.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a school as a place of instruction; a master as a teacher; learning as acquired knowledge; a province as an ecclesiastical district under a metropolitan; and a use as a customary liturgical practice.
webster_full: SCHOOL, n. A place or house in which persons are instructed in arts, science, languages or any species of learning.
MASTER, n. A director, head or chief; one who teaches; an instructor; a teacher of a school.
LEARNING, n. The knowledge of principles or facts received by instruction or study; acquired knowledge or ideas in any branch of science or literature.
PROVINCE, n. The division of a country; a jurisdiction; the district over which an archbishop has authority.
USE, n. A customary practice; habitual employment; the manner of using; a rite or liturgical custom.
scriptures: And the things that thou hast heard of me among many witnesses, the same commit thou to faithful men, who shall be able to teach others also.
So then faith cometh by hearing, and hearing by the word of God.
Eph 4:11
And he gave some, apostles; and some, prophets; and some, evangelists; and some, pastors and teachers;
Pro 9:9
Give instruction to a wise man, and he will be yet wiser: teach a just man, and he will increase in learning.
corruption_summary: Northern archbishopric of England whose cathedral school taught Alcuin, who carried Northumbrian learning to Charlemagne's court and re-founded Frankish education.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the succession of teachers, which is how learning in the church actually travels. Paul commands it with four links visible in one sentence: what Timothy heard from Paul he is to commit “to faithful men, who shall be able to teach others also” (2Ti 2:2). Aelbert taught Alcuin, Alcuin taught Hrabanus Maurus, Hrabanus taught the ninth century, and the chain is of exactly that kind.

The second paragraph names the live temptation, which is to expect renewal from an institution rather than from men who can teach. Christ's gift to the church is a list of persons, not of structures, “and some, pastors and teachers” (Eph 4:11), and the mechanism by which faith arises is a thing said and heard: “So then faith cometh by hearing, and hearing by the word of God” (Rom 10:17). Solomon states the condition on the receiving end, which no school can supply: “Give instruction to a wise man, and he will be yet wiser” (Pro 9:9). York had the library, the masters and, in Alcuin, the wise man.

roots_lines: Greek paratithemi (G3908) — to commit as a deposit; “the same commit thou to faithful men”, 2 Timothy 2:2.
Greek didaskalos (G1320) — a teacher, an instructor; “and some, pastors and teachers”, Ephesians 4:11.
Greek akoe (G0189) — the act of hearing, a report; “So then faith cometh by hearing”, Romans 10:17.
Greek rhema (G4487) — a spoken word; “and hearing by the word of God”, Romans 10:17.
Hebrew chakam (H2450) — wise, skilful; “Give instruction to a wise man, and he will be yet wiser”, Proverbs 9:9.
usage: “the same commit thou to faithful men” (2Ti 2:2) — the succession of teachers, commanded.
“So then faith cometh by hearing” (Rom 10:17) — the mechanism a school serves.
“Give instruction to a wise man, and he will be yet wiser” (Pro 9:9) — the condition no school supplies.

pos: n. (the northern English prince-bishopric built around the shrine of Cuthbert, holding the bones of Bede and the Lindisfarne Gospels)
etymology: From Old English dun, a hill, and Old Norse holmr, an island, for the rock in the loop of the Wear.
biblical_def: Durham was founded in 995 when the community of Lindisfarne, driven inland by Viking raids and wandering for a century with the body of Cuthbert, settled on the rock in the loop of the Wear. The cathedral was begun in 1093 and is the finest Norman building in England; its bishops held the office of prince-bishop with regalian powers over the county palatine until 1836, raising armies against the Scots. The relics of Bede were brought here in the eleventh century, and the Lindisfarne Gospels were made in the community that founded it. Durham produced John Cosin, bishop after the Restoration, and had earlier been the see of Cuthbert Tunstall, who refused the Edwardian reforms and was deprived. The dictionary records Durham for the hundred years of wandering. A congregation carrying the body of its dead bishop from place to place for three generations, keeping its books and its daily office, is the church in its most reduced form and the dictionary thinks it instructive.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a shrine as a case for sacred things; palatine as possessing royal privileges; a see as the seat of a bishop; perseverance as continuance in a state of grace; and office as a form of divine service.
webster_full: SHRINE, n. A case, box or receptacle for depositing sacred things; a sacred place; an altar.
PALATINE, a. Pertaining to a palace; possessing royal privileges; as a county palatine.
SEE, n. The seat of episcopal power; a diocese; the jurisdiction of a bishop.
PERSEVERANCE, n. Persistence in any thing undertaken; in theology, continuance in a state of grace to a state of glory.
OFFICE, n. In liturgics, a formulary of devotion; the daily service of the church.
scriptures: Heb 13:7
Remember them which have the rule over you, who have spoken unto you the word of God: whose faith follow, considering the end of their conversation.
I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith:
Heb 12:1

Wherefore seeing we also are compassed about with so great a cloud of witnesses, let us lay aside every weight, and the sin which doth so easily beset us, and let us run with patience the race that is set before us,

And I heard a voice from heaven saying unto me, Write, Blessed are the dead which die in the Lord from henceforth: Yea, saith the Spirit, that they may rest from their labours; and their works do follow them.
corruption_summary: Northern English prince-bishopric founded in 995 by the wandering community of Lindisfarne, holding the shrine of Cuthbert and the bones of Bede.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the shrine, which is where the dictionary must be careful, because the thing the Lindisfarne community actually did was faithful and the thing it became was not. Carrying a bishop's body with them was an act of love for a man and for a rule of life; enshrining it for pilgrims to pay at is another matter. Scripture directs the right use of a dead teacher, and it is imitation of his faith rather than attendance at his tomb: “Remember them which have the rule over you, who have spoken unto you the word of God: whose faith follow” (Heb 13:7).

The second paragraph names the principle to recover. The honour Scripture pays a finished ministry is to its course and its keeping, “I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith” (2Ti 4:7); the dead are described as resting from labours that follow them rather than as dispensing favours, “Blessed are the dead which die in the Lord” (Rev 14:13); and the living are pictured running inside a crowd of such witnesses, “compassed about with so great a cloud of witnesses” (Heb 12:1). A cloud of witnesses is a congregation to be imitated. It is not a reliquary.
roots_summary: Greek mimeomai, to imitate, from mimetes (G3402); Greek dromos (G1408), a course; Greek nephos (G3509), a cloud.

Greek dromos (G1408) — a race, a course; “I have finished my course”, 2 Timothy 4:7.

usage: “whose faith follow” (Heb 13:7) — the right use of a dead teacher.
“I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith” (2Ti 4:7) — the honour Scripture pays a ministry.
“Blessed are the dead which die in the Lord” (Rev 14:13) — the dead rest; they do not dispense.

pos: n. (the Devon see besieged in the Prayer Book Rebellion of 1549, and the diocese of Miles Coverdale from 1551 to 1553)
etymology: From Latin Isca, the river, with Old English ceaster, a Roman fort.
biblical_def: Exeter is the cathedral city of Devon, a Roman town and a see since 1050. In the summer of 1549 the western rising known as the Prayer Book Rebellion besieged it for five weeks: the Cornish and Devon rebels demanded the restoration of the Latin mass and the old ceremonies, and their articles included the complaint that they did not understand the new English service, some of them being Cornish speakers who understood no English either. The rising was put down with considerable slaughter at Sampford Courtenay and Clyst Heath. In 1551 Miles Coverdale, who had made the first complete printed English Bible in 1535, was appointed bishop of Exeter, and was deprived on Mary's accession and went into exile. The dictionary records Exeter because the rebels' complaint deserves an answer rather than a sneer, and because the answer is the principle they had been denied: a service in the tongue the worshipper actually speaks.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a liturgy as a form of prayers; a rebellion as an open resistance to lawful authority; vernacular as native to a country; a grievance as a wrong suffered; and intelligible as capable of being understood.
webster_full: LITURGY, n. A formulary of public devotions; all the prescribed services of a church, as distinct from the sermon.
REBELLION, n. An open and avowed renunciation of the authority of the government to which one owes allegiance.
VERNACULAR, a. Native; belonging to the country of one's birth; as one's vernacular tongue.
GRIEVANCE, n. That which causes grief or uneasiness; a wrong suffered; injury, hardship or oppression.
INTELLIGIBLE, a. That may be understood or comprehended; clear; plain.
scriptures: So likewise ye, except ye utter by the tongue words easy to be understood, how shall it be known what is spoken? for ye shall speak into the air.
Act 2:8
And how hear we every man in our own tongue, wherein we were born?
Else when thou shalt bless with the spirit, how shall he that occupieth the room of the unlearned say Amen at thy giving of thanks, seeing he understandeth not what thou sayest?
Neh 8:8
So they read in the book in the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading.
corruption_summary: Devon see besieged for five weeks in the 1549 Prayer Book Rebellion, and from 1551 the diocese of Miles Coverdale, maker of the first complete printed English Bible.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is a service nobody understands, and the dictionary says the Cornish rebels of 1549 were half right. Their complaint was that the new English liturgy was a strange thing to them; what they did not see was that the Latin they were defending had been a strange thing to their grandfathers for nine hundred years. Paul rules on the whole question in a chapter devoted to it, and the rule is comprehension: unless words are spoken plainly, “how shall it be known what is spoken? for ye shall speak into the air” (1Co 14:9).

The second paragraph names the principle to recover and extends it in the rebels' own favour. Paul ties the congregation's amen to its understanding, asking of the unlearned hearer, “say Amen at thy giving of thanks, seeing he understandeth not what thou sayest” (1Co 14:16), and Pentecost puts the ideal as every man in his own tongue, “how hear we every man in our own tongue, wherein we were born?” (Act 2:8). On that principle the Cornish should have been given a Cornish liturgy, which they never were, and the Levites' method is what they needed, “and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading” (Neh 8:8). The dictionary regards the failure to translate into Cornish as a real fault of the English Reformation.

“seeing he understandeth not what thou sayest” (1Co 14:16) — why the congregation's amen requires comprehension.

pos: n. (the largest medieval English diocese, the see of Robert Grosseteste and the diocese in which Wycliffe and Oxford lay)
etymology: From Latin Lindum Colonia, the colony at Lindum, from a British name for the pool.
biblical_def: Lincoln held the largest diocese in medieval England, running from the Humber to the Thames and including Oxford, so that every question raised in the university was in the end a Lincoln matter. Its greatest bishop was Robert Grosseteste, from 1235 to 1253, a scholar of Greek and of optics, translator of Aristotle and of the Greek fathers, and a reformer of ferocious energy: he visited every parish in the diocese, deprived incompetent clergy, insisted that rectors reside and preach, and in 1250 delivered at the papal court a sermon denouncing the curia's practice of granting English benefices to absentee Italians as the cause of the people's ruin. He refused a papal provision in 1253 in writing. The dictionary records Grosseteste as the model of what a bishop should be and had almost never been: resident, learned, pastoral and willing to tell Rome to its face that it was destroying souls for revenue.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a benefice as an ecclesiastical living; residence as the act of dwelling in a place; visitation as the inspection of a church by a superior; provision as the appointment to a benefice; and remonstrance as a strong representation of reasons against a measure.
webster_full: BENEFICE, n. Literally, a benefit, advantage or kindness; in church affairs, an ecclesiastical living; a church endowed with a revenue.
RESIDENCE, n. The act of abiding or dwelling in a place for some continuance of time; the place of abode.
VISITATION, n. A judicial visit or examination of a corporation or church, by a superior, to inquire into its manner of conducting affairs.
PROVISION, n. In church affairs, the appointment of a successor to a benefice not yet vacant, by the pope.
REMONSTRANCE, n. Show; discovery; a strong representation of reasons against a measure, either in person or in writing.
scriptures: Eze 33:7
So thou, O son of man, I have set thee a watchman unto the house of Israel; therefore thou shalt hear the word at my mouth, and warn them from me.
Mal 2:7
For the priest's lips should keep knowledge, and they should seek the law at his mouth: for he is the messenger of the LORD of hosts.
For I have not shunned to declare unto you all the counsel of God.
Feed the flock of God which is among you, taking the oversight thereof, not by constraint, but willingly; not for filthy lucre, but of a ready mind;
corruption_summary: Largest medieval English diocese, see of Robert Grosseteste, who denounced to the papal court the granting of English benefices to absentee Italians.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the benefice held for its income by a man who never sees the parish, which Grosseteste attacked at the source and which outlived him by three centuries. A cure of souls given as a salary to an absentee is not a minor administrative fault; it leaves a village without preaching for a generation. Ezekiel states the office that such an arrangement abolishes, and it is a duty of speech: “thou shalt hear the word at my mouth, and warn them from me” (Eze 33:7).

The second paragraph names the principle to recover. The priest's mouth is the people's access to instruction, “For the priest's lips should keep knowledge, and they should seek the law at his mouth” (Mal 2:7); Paul's claim on his own ministry is completeness, “For I have not shunned to declare unto you all the counsel of God” (Act 20:27); and Peter forbids both compulsion and greed in the motive while commanding the work itself, to feed the flock “not by constraint, but willingly; not for filthy lucre, but of a ready mind” (1Pe 5:2). Grosseteste visited every parish in the biggest diocese in England. The dictionary notes that this was thought eccentric.

“For the priest's lips should keep knowledge” (Mal 2:7) — the people's access to instruction.
“For I have not shunned to declare unto you all the counsel of God” (Act 20:27) — the standard of completeness.

pos: n. (the old West Saxon capital and wealthiest English see, held by Stephen Gardiner and later by Lancelot Andrewes)
etymology: From Latin Venta Belgarum, with Old English ceaster, a Roman fort.
biblical_def: Winchester was the capital of Wessex and so of England before the Conquest, and its see was the richest in the kingdom. Its bishops were therefore men of state. Stephen Gardiner, bishop from 1531, supported Henry the Eighth against the pope, opposed the Edwardian reformation, was imprisoned through that reign, and as Mary's chancellor restored the heresy laws under which Cranmer, Ridley, Latimer and some three hundred others were burned. Lancelot Andrewes, bishop from 1619, was one of the chief translators of the Authorized Version, a preacher of great weight and a man of famously private devotion whose Preces Privatae was found after his death. The Winchester Bible, a twelfth-century illuminated manuscript, is the largest surviving English Romanesque Bible. The dictionary records Winchester for the contrast between its two most famous bishops, and for the observation that the one who burned men held the chancellorship and the one who made the Bible held no office of state at all.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a chancellor as a high judicial officer; devotion as solemn attention to God in worship; a translator as one who renders into another language; preferment as advancement to a higher office; and privacy as a state of seclusion.
webster_full: CHANCELLOR, n. A high officer of state; the chief judge of the court of chancery; in England, a minister of great power.
DEVOTION, n. A solemn attention to the Supreme Being in worship; a yielding of the heart and affections to God.
TRANSLATOR, n. One who renders a discourse or writing from one language into another.
PREFERMENT, n. Advancement to a higher office or dignity; promotion; a superior place or office.
PRIVACY, n. A state of being in retirement from company or from the knowledge or observation of others; secrecy.
scriptures: Mat 6:6
But thou, when thou prayest, enter into thy closet, and when thou hast shut thy door, pray to thy Father which is in secret; and thy Father which seeth in secret shall reward thee openly.
Tit 1:9
Holding fast the faithful word as he hath been taught, that he may be able by sound doctrine both to exhort and to convince the gainsayers.
Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season; reprove, rebuke, exhort with all longsuffering and doctrine.
Mat 7:16
Ye shall know them by their fruits. Do men gather grapes of thorns, or figs of thistles?
corruption_summary: Old West Saxon capital and wealthiest English see, held by Stephen Gardiner, who restored the heresy laws, and later by Lancelot Andrewes, translator of the Authorized Version.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the bishop as minister of state, which Winchester's wealth made almost unavoidable and which produced Gardiner. A man who holds the chancellorship and a diocese together will find that the diocese serves the chancellorship, and in Gardiner's case it served it by supplying a legal machinery for burning. Christ gives the test that settles between two such men without reference to their rank: “Ye shall know them by their fruits” (Mat 7:16).

The second paragraph names the principle to recover, which Andrewes illustrates. His private prayers were not written to be read; they were found. Christ commands exactly that, “But thou, when thou prayest, enter into thy closet, and when thou hast shut thy door, pray to thy Father which is in secret” (Mat 6:6). And a bishop's public competence is defined by the deposit and the pulpit rather than by the council chamber: he must be “Holding fast the faithful word as he hath been taught” (Tit 1:9), and the charge laid on him is “Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season” (2Ti 4:2). Andrewes gave England a Bible. Gardiner gave it a statute.

“pray to thy Father which is in secret” (Mat 6:6) — what Andrewes was doing when nobody was looking.

pos: n. (the north-western English see whose mystery-play cycle was performed by the city guilds until its suppression in 1575)
etymology: From Old English ceaster, from Latin castra, a camp, for the legionary fortress of Deva.
biblical_def: Chester was the Roman legionary fortress of Deva, a walled city on the Dee, and was made a see in 1541 out of the dissolved abbey of Saint Werburgh. Its chief interest to this dictionary is the Chester cycle, one of the four surviving English mystery-play cycles, twenty-four plays running from the creation to the last judgment, performed over three days at Whitsun by the city's craft guilds, each guild taking a play suited to its trade, so that the water-carriers played the flood and the bakers the last supper. The cycle was performed into the fifteen-seventies and suppressed in 1575 by the archbishop of York and the city's own reforming mayor. The dictionary records Chester because the suppression raises the hardest question in the Reformed account of worship and art, and because the answer has to be stated with care: the plays were not worship, the objection to them was the representation of the persons of the Godhead, and that objection is sound.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a pageant as a show or spectacle; a guild as a fraternity or company; a mystery as a trade or craft, and also a dramatic representation of sacred history; representation as the act of exhibiting; and suppression as the act of putting down.
webster_full: PAGEANT, n. A statue in a show; any show, spectacle or ceremonial exhibition; something showy without substance.
GUILD, n. A society, fraternity or corporation associated for some purpose; a company of tradesmen.
MYSTERY, n. A trade; a calling; any mechanical occupation which requires skill in performing the manual operations.
REPRESENTATION, n. The act of representing; exhibition by a dramatic performance; a likeness or image.
SUPPRESSION, n. The act of putting an end to or crushing; concealment; the act of keeping back or restraining.
scriptures: Exo 20:4
Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image, or any likeness of any thing that is in heaven above, or that is in the earth beneath, or that is in the water under the earth:
Deu 4:15
Take ye therefore good heed unto yourselves; for ye saw no manner of similitude on the day that the LORD spake unto you in Horeb out of the midst of the fire:
So then faith cometh by hearing, and hearing by the word of God.
For after that in the wisdom of God the world by wisdom knew not God, it pleased God by the foolishness of preaching to save them that believe.
corruption_summary: North-western English see whose twenty-four play Whitsun cycle was performed by the city guilds until its suppression in 1575.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the representation of God, and the dictionary states the objection precisely because the easy version of it is wrong. There is nothing unlawful in a play, in a craft guild, or in telling the history of redemption in the street. The objection to the cycles is that men stood on carts and played God the Father and God the Son, which is a likeness made of the One who commanded that none be made: “Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image, or any likeness of any thing that is in heaven above” (Exo 20:4). Moses grounds it in what Israel saw at Horeb, which was nothing: “ye saw no manner of similitude” (Deu 4:15).

The second paragraph names the principle to recover, which is the appointed means. God has chosen a method for making himself known that looks weaker than a pageant and is not: “it pleased God by the foolishness of preaching to save them that believe” (1Co 1:21). The mechanism is stated flatly, “So then faith cometh by hearing, and hearing by the word of God” (Rom 10:17). The dictionary adds that something real was lost at Chester in 1575, namely a civic, popular, annual telling of the whole Bible story that the ordinary trades owned; and that the remedy was never to supply a substitute, which is a fault the Reformed tradition should own.

Greek moria (G3472) — foolishness; “the foolishness of preaching”, 1 Corinthians 1:21.
Greek akoe (G0189) — hearing, a report; “So then faith cometh by hearing”, Romans 10:17.

“ye saw no manner of similitude” (Deu 4:15) — the ground of the prohibition.
“by the foolishness of preaching to save them that believe” (1Co 1:21) — the appointed means instead.

pos: n. (the western English see of the Mappa Mundi and the chained library, and the home diocese of Nicholas Hereford, translator of the Lollard Bible)
etymology: From Old English here, an army, and ford, a river crossing.
biblical_def: Hereford is a border see on the Welsh march, founded about 676, whose cathedral keeps two remarkable things: the Mappa Mundi of about 1300, the largest surviving medieval world map, with Jerusalem at its centre and the earthly paradise at its edge, and a chained library of some fifteen hundred volumes, the largest surviving example of books secured to their shelves by chain. The county also gave its name to Nicholas Hereford, an Oxford doctor and associate of Wycliffe, who translated a large part of the Old Testament for the earlier Lollard version before he was excommunicated, imprisoned in Rome, escaped, recanted under pressure in 1391, and ended as a persecutor of his former colleagues. The dictionary records Hereford for the chains and for Nicholas together. A book chained to a shelf is still a book a man may read; what the Lollard translation attempted was to take the chain off the whole Bible, and the fate of the man who did most of the Old Testament is a sober warning.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a chain as a series of links; a library as a collection of books; a map as a representation of the earth's surface; apostasy as a departure from one's faith; and a version as a translation.
webster_full: CHAIN, n. A series of links or rings connected; that which binds; a bond; a series of things linked together.
LIBRARY, n. A collection of books belonging to a private person, or to a public institution or a company.
MAP, n. A representation of the surface of the earth, or of any part of it, drawn on paper or other material.
APOSTASY, n. An abandonment of what one has professed; a total desertion or departure from one's faith.
VERSION, n. A translation; the act of translating; the rendering of a work from one language into another.
scriptures: Wherein I suffer trouble, as an evil doer, even unto bonds; but the word of God is not bound.
The entrance of thy words giveth light; it giveth understanding unto the simple.
Wherefore let him that thinketh he standeth take heed lest he fall.
Watch and pray, that ye enter not into temptation: the spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak.
corruption_summary: Western English see of the Mappa Mundi and the chained library, and home diocese of Nicholas Hereford, Lollard Old Testament translator who later recanted and persecuted.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is not the chain on the library shelf, which merely kept expensive books from being stolen, but the chain on the text itself, which is what the Lollards attacked. Paul's sentence from prison is the standing answer to every form of that restraint: “but the word of God is not bound” (2Ti 2:9). What the Lollard version was for is stated by the psalmist in one line, and it is the reason translation is never a luxury: “The entrance of thy words giveth light; it giveth understanding unto the simple” (Psa 119:130).

The second paragraph names the principle to recover, and it is about Nicholas Hereford rather than about the books. A man who translated much of the Old Testament into English, was imprisoned for it in Rome and escaped, recanted in 1391 and afterwards helped hunt the men he had worked with. Paul's warning is addressed to exactly the confidence that precedes such a fall: “let him that thinketh he standeth take heed lest he fall” (1Co 10:12). Christ names the remedy and the reason in one sentence in the garden: “Watch and pray, that ye enter not into temptation: the spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak” (Mat 26:41). The dictionary keeps his name with his work and with his end, because leaving out either would be dishonest.

“it giveth understanding unto the simple” (Psa 119:130) — what the Lollard version was for.

pos: n. (the Leicestershire parish where John Wycliffe was rector, wrote his last works and died in 1384, and whose bones were burned in 1428)
etymology: From Old English, perhaps the enclosure by the river Hlutre, the clear stream, with worth, an enclosure.
biblical_def: Lutterworth is a small market town in Leicestershire, and its parish was John Wycliffe's. Presented to the rectory in 1374, he withdrew there after the condemnation of his eucharistic teaching at Oxford in 1381 and spent his last three years writing: the Trialogus, a great mass of sermons, and the organising of the English Bible that his associates Nicholas Hereford and John Purvey carried through. He suffered a stroke while hearing mass in his own church and died on the thirty-first of December 1384. The council of Constance condemned his memory in 1415, and in 1428 his bones were exhumed on papal order, burned, and the ashes thrown into the river Swift. The dictionary records Lutterworth because the last three years are the ones that mattered. A condemned man in a country parish, writing sermons and superintending a translation, did more to the church of the next two centuries than the council that dug him up.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a rector as a clergyman who has the charge of a parish; exhumation as the digging up of what is buried; posterity as succeeding generations; condemnation as the act of pronouncing guilty; and a translation as a rendering into another language.
webster_full: RECTOR, n. A ruler or governor; a clergyman who has the charge and cure of a parish, and has the tithes of it.
EXHUMATION, n. The digging up of a dead body that has been buried; the disinterring of a corpse.
POSTERITY, n. Descendants; children, grandchildren and succeeding generations; opposed to ancestors.
CONDEMNATION, n. The act of condemning; the judicial act of declaring one guilty and dooming him to punishment.
TRANSLATION, n. The act of turning into another language; the rendering of a discourse or writing into another tongue.
scriptures: So shall my word be that goeth forth out of my mouth: it shall not return unto me void, but it shall accomplish that which I please, and it shall prosper in the thing whereto I sent it.
Is not my word like as a fire? saith the LORD; and like a hammer that breaketh the rock in pieces?
Wherein I suffer trouble, as an evil doer, even unto bonds; but the word of God is not bound.
Joh 5:39
Search the scriptures; for in them ye think ye have eternal life: and they are they which testify of me.
corruption_summary: Leicestershire parish where Wycliffe was rector, wrote his last works and organised the English Bible, and whose bones were exhumed and burned in 1428.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the attempt to destroy a man's influence by destroying his remains, which the church attempted at Lutterworth in 1428 forty-four years after his death. It did not work, and the dictionary thinks the failure instructive rather than merely ironic. What Wycliffe had set going was a text in English, and a text is not in the grave. The promise attached to the word is about effect rather than about the safety of the man who carried it: “it shall not return unto me void, but it shall accomplish that which I please” (Isa 55:11).

The second paragraph names the principle to recover. Jeremiah describes a force that an exhumation order cannot reach, “Is not my word like as a fire? saith the LORD; and like a hammer that breaketh the rock in pieces?” (Jer 23:29), and Paul writes from custody about the one thing in the room that is not under sentence: “but the word of God is not bound” (2Ti 2:9). The command Wycliffe spent his last years making possible for Englishmen is Christ's own, “Search the scriptures; for in them ye think ye have eternal life” (Joh 5:39). Ashes went into the Swift, the Swift into the Avon, and the English Bible into every parish in the country within a hundred and fifty years.

pos: n. (the English county town of John Bunyan's congregation and of the gaol in which he spent twelve years and wrote)
etymology: From Old English, the ford of Beda, a personal name, with ford, a river crossing.
biblical_def: Bedford on the Ouse is the county town of Bedfordshire and the place of John Bunyan. Converted in the early sixteen-fifties and joined to the open-membership congregation gathered by John Gifford at Saint John's, he began preaching in 1655, was arrested in November 1660 under the restored Act of Uniformity for holding a meeting, and refused the condition of silence; he was held in the county gaol for twelve years to 1672 and again briefly in 1677. In prison he wrote Grace Abounding and began The Pilgrim's Progress, published in 1678, which has been translated into more languages than any English book but the Bible. He was afterwards pastor of the Bedford church until his death in 1688. The dictionary records Bedford because Bunyan's refusal was of a very specific kind: he was not asked to deny the faith, only to stop preaching, and he answered that if he were out today he would preach tomorrow.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a gaol as a prison; conformity as compliance with an established form; an allegory as a figurative discourse; a tinker as a mender of brass kettles; and a conventicle as a private religious assembly.
webster_full: GAOL, n. A prison; a building or place for the confinement of debtors and criminals.
CONFORMITY, n. Correspondence with a model or pattern; compliance with the usages of the established church.
ALLEGORY, n. A figurative sentence or discourse, in which the principal subject is described by another subject resembling it in its properties and circumstances.
TINKER, n. A mender of brass kettles, pans and the like; an itinerant mender of household vessels.
CONVENTICLE, n. An assembly for religious worship; appropriately, an assembly of dissenters, so called in contempt.
scriptures: Act 5:42
And daily in the temple, and in every house, they ceased not to teach and preach Jesus Christ.
Act 4:20
For we cannot but speak the things which we have seen and heard.
Php 1:12
But I would ye should understand, brethren, that the things which happened unto me have fallen out rather unto the furtherance of the gospel;
And others had trial of cruel mockings and scourgings, yea, moreover of bonds and imprisonment:
corruption_summary: English county town of Bunyan's open-membership congregation and of the gaol where he spent twelve years and began The Pilgrim's Progress.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the law that permits a man his belief and forbids him his voice, which is the exact shape of the Act under which Bunyan was held. He was never required to recant; he was required to be quiet, and the dictionary insists that this is not a lesser demand. Peter and John gave the only possible answer to it: “For we cannot but speak the things which we have seen and heard” (Act 4:20), and the apostles' practice under prohibition was simply to continue, for “daily in the temple, and in every house, they ceased not to teach and preach Jesus Christ” (Act 5:42).

The second paragraph names the principle to recover, which is what God does with a prison. Paul found that his confinement served the thing it was meant to stop, “the things which happened unto me have fallen out rather unto the furtherance of the gospel” (Php 1:12). Hebrews lists imprisonment among the honours of faith rather than its interruptions, naming those who “had trial of cruel mockings and scourgings, yea, moreover of bonds and imprisonment” (Heb 11:36). The dictionary observes that twelve years in Bedford gaol produced the most widely read book in the English language after the Bible, and that no plan of Bunyan's could have arranged it.

pos: n. (the Somerset abbey of the Joseph of Arimathea legend, whose last abbot Richard Whiting was hanged on the Tor in 1539)
etymology: From Old English Glaestingaburh, the stronghold of the Glaestingas, a people of the Somerset levels.
biblical_def: Glastonbury was the richest abbey in England after Westminster, a foundation of great antiquity on an island in the Somerset levels, where Dunstan was abbot in the tenth century and from which much of the English monastic revival came. It also carried a legend: that Joseph of Arimathea came there with the cup of the last supper and planted a thorn that flowered at Christmas, and that Arthur was buried in the grounds, a claim the monks announced in 1191. At the dissolution the abbey's last abbot, Richard Whiting, an old man, was convicted of treason on evidence that would not now be accepted and hanged, drawn and quartered on Glastonbury Tor in November 1539 with two of his monks. In Edward the Sixth's reign the site housed a colony of Flemish Protestant weavers. The dictionary records Glastonbury for the legend and for the hanging, and refuses to let the first excuse the second: a fabricated relic tradition is a sin, and the judicial murder of an old man for his house's revenues is another one.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an abbey as a monastery; dissolution as the act of breaking up; a legend as a chronicle of a saint's life, often fabulous; treason as the betrayal of one's government; and attainder as the extinction of civil rights on sentence of death.
webster_full: ABBEY, n. A monastery or society of persons of either sex, secluded from the world and devoted to religion; the house occupied by such a society.
DISSOLUTION, n. The act of liquefying; the breaking up of an assembly; destruction; the separation of the parts of a body.
LEGEND, n. A chronicle or register of the lives of saints, formerly read at matins; any memorial or relation; an idle or fabulous story.
TREASON, n. The offense of attempting to overthrow the government of the state to which the offender owes allegiance.
ATTAINDER, n. The judgment of death, or the state of being so condemned, with extinction of civil rights.
scriptures: Prove all things; hold fast that which is good.
Neither give heed to fables and endless genealogies, which minister questions, rather than godly edifying which is in faith: so do.
Thou shalt not bear false witness against thy neighbour.
Pro 31:8
Open thy mouth for the dumb in the cause of all such as are appointed to destruction.
corruption_summary: Richest Somerset abbey, carrying the Joseph of Arimathea legend, whose last abbot Richard Whiting was hanged on the Tor in 1539 for treason.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is double, and the dictionary names both and lets neither cancel the other. Glastonbury manufactured a relic tradition: Joseph of Arimathea, the thorn, the grave of Arthur discovered conveniently after a fire had destroyed the church and money was needed. Paul warns Timothy against exactly this class of material, charging him to forbid men to “give heed to fables and endless genealogies” (1Ti 1:4). The rule is examination instead: “Prove all things; hold fast that which is good” (1Th 5:21).

The second paragraph names the second sin, which was the crown's. Richard Whiting was an old man tried on manufactured evidence by commissioners who had already valued his abbey, and his execution on the hill above his own house was a judicial murder. The ninth commandment governs the trial: “Thou shalt not bear false witness against thy neighbour” (Exo 20:16), and Solomon imposes a duty on everyone else in the room, which nobody at Glastonbury discharged: “Open thy mouth for the dumb in the cause of all such as are appointed to destruction” (Pro 31:8). The dictionary holds that a reformation which seizes an abbey for its revenues and hangs its abbot has not reformed anything.

“Thou shalt not bear false witness against thy neighbour” (Exo 20:16) — the commandment the trial broke.
